name: Syntactic Diversity Score
description: Quantifies diversity of syntactic structures used — AI text often relies on a narrow set of syntactic templates.
algorithm: Parse Tree Template Diversity and Syntactic Repertoire Analysis
mechanism:
This method applies Syntactic Diversity Score analysis for AI-generated content detection:

1. **Parse Tree Template Extraction**: Each sentence is parsed into a constituency tree, and the tree is abstracted into a syntactic template by retaining only phrase-level structure (S → NP VP, VP → VBD NP PP, etc.) while removing lexical content. This produces a structural fingerprint for each sentence. The method counts unique templates and computes: (a) syntactic type-token ratio (STTR) — unique templates / total sentences. Human text STTR: 0.70–0.90 (high diversity — most sentences have unique structures). AI text STTR: 0.45–0.65 (lower diversity — many sentences share the same template). (b) Template frequency distribution — the shape of the distribution of template frequencies. Human: flat distribution (most templates used 1–2 times). AI: concentrated distribution (few templates used 3–5 times each, dominating the text). (c) Hapax template ratio — the proportion of templates appearing exactly once. Human: 0.60–0.80. AI: 0.35–0.55.

2. **Clause-Level Syntactic Patterns**: Beyond full-sentence templates, the method analyzes clause-level syntactic diversity: (a) clause type distribution — the proportion of main clauses, relative clauses, adverbial clauses, noun clauses, and participial clauses. Human text uses 5–7 clause types with no single type exceeding 40% of all clauses. AI text uses 3–5 types with the dominant type (usually main clause + relative clause) exceeding 50%. (b) Subordination diversity — the variety of subordinating conjunctions used. Human: 6–12 different subordinators per 1000 words. AI: 3–7 (relying heavily on 'that', 'which', 'because'). (c) VP complexity diversity — the range of verb phrase structures (simple, progressive, passive, modal + infinitive, complex). Human VP type count: 8–14 per 1000 words. AI: 5–9.

3. **Syntactic Novelty and Repetition Detection**: The method identifies syntactic repetition patterns that signal AI generation: (a) template recycling — using the same syntactic template in consecutive sentences. Human consecutive repetition rate: 5–12%. AI: 15–30%. The method specifically flags 'syntactic echoes' where 3+ consecutive sentences share the same template. Human echo rate: 1–3% of sentence triples. AI: 5–12%. (b) Paragraph-initial template — the syntactic template used for the first sentence of each paragraph. Human text shows 60–80% unique paragraph-initial templates. AI: 35–55% (paragraphs start with repetitive structures). (c) Listing template — the structure used in enumerated or listed items. Human varied listing structures: 'First...Second...Third', 'Moreover...Additionally...Furthermore', mixed with non-formulaic transitions. AI: highly formulaic listing with 2–3 repeated connecting structures.

4. **Syntactic Complexity Distribution**: The method measures the spread of syntactic complexity rather than its mean: (a) sentence complexity histogram — the distribution of sentences across 5 complexity bands (simple, compound, complex, compound-complex, multi-embedded). Human distribution entropy: 1.8–2.2 bits (spread across bands). AI: 1.2–1.6 bits (concentrated in 1–2 bands). (b) Maximum embedding depth distribution — the range of maximum embedding depths across sentences. Human depth range: 1–8 levels (wide range from simple to deeply embedded). AI depth range: 2–5 levels (compressed range, avoiding both very simple and very complex structures). (c) Cross-sentence complexity transitions — the probability matrix of moving from one complexity band to another. Human matrices show off-diagonal entries of 0.15–0.25 (frequent band switching). AI matrices show diagonal dominance > 0.40 (sentences tend to stay in the same complexity band).
parameters:
STTR human: 0.70–0.90
STTR AI: 0.45–0.65
Hapax template ratio human: 0.60–0.80
Hapax template ratio AI: 0.35–0.55
Clause type dominant human: <40%
Clause type dominant AI: >50%
Consecutive template repeat human: 5–12%
Consecutive template repeat AI: 15–30%
Paragraph-initial unique human: 60–80%
Paragraph-initial unique AI: 35–55%
Complexity distribution entropy human: 1.8–2.2 bits
Complexity distribution entropy AI: 1.2–1.6 bits
Minimum sentences: 15
accuracy: 80–87% accuracy detecting AI-generated text through syntactic diversity analysis. STTR achieves AUC of 0.86. Template recycling detection provides F1-score of 0.83. Complexity distribution entropy adds 3–4% improvement. Performs best on essays, articles, and multi-paragraph text with 20+ sentences.
source: Foster, J. & van Genabith, J. (2008). Parser Evaluation and the BNC: Evaluating 4 Constituency Parsers with 3 Metrics. LREC 2008.
useCase: Detecting AI-generated essays through repetitive syntactic templates. Evaluating writing sophistication through structural variety. Identifying AI-written reports through paragraph-opening repetition. Assessing stylistic quality through syntactic repertoire analysis.
strengths:
• Parse tree templates capture deep structural patterns beyond surface length
• STTR is a simple, interpretable metric highly correlated with AI detection
• Template recycling detection catches formulaic AI writing
• Complexity distribution analysis reveals missing structural extremes
• Applicable to most prose genres with sufficient length
limitations:
• Constituency parser accuracy affects template extraction
• Some genres (legal, technical) naturally have low syntactic diversity
• Very short texts may not contain enough sentences for meaningful STTR
• Different parsers may produce different template inventories
• Advanced AI models increasingly vary syntactic structures
